title: Date Palm Overview: Phoenix dactylifera
description: The date palm, Phoenix dactylifera, is a flowering plant in the palm family Arecaceae, cultivated across northern Africa, the Middle East, South Asia, and parts of the Americas for its sweet edible fruit, the date. Published references describe a tree growing about 23 metres tall, with a single slender trunk marked by the pruned stubs of old leaf bases and crowned by large pinnate fronds about 5 metres long. It is one of the oldest cultivated fruit trees, with archaeological evidence of date cultivation in Arabia from the 6th millennium BCE, and it remains emblematic of oasis agriculture. A mature date palm bears large hanging bunches of fruit, each bunch holding more than 1,000 individual dates and weighing 8 kilograms or more, according to Britannica. The fruit is a one-seeded drupe, usually oblong, varying in shape, size, colour, and flesh consistency with variety and growing conditions. Palms begin to bear fruit in 4 to 5 years and reach full bearing at 10 to 15 years, yielding 40 to 80 kilograms or more per tree, and individual palms are known to live as long as 150 years, although commercial groves replace trees earlier as production declines. Dates are eaten fresh, dried, and processed, and dried dates contain roughly 63 to 64 percent sugar by mass, which is why they keep well and travel well. The palm also gives fibre, timber, fronds for weaving, and shade for crops grown beneath it, so a single species supports food, material, and shelter uses in the same grove. Figures in this record are stated as published ranges, as of 2026-10-26, because height, yield, and lifespan vary with variety, water, and care.

title: Palm Biology: Roots, Trunk, Fronds, Flowers, and Fruit
description: The date palm is a monocotyledon, so it does not grow a true woody trunk with annual rings the way an oak does. Its stem is a column of persistent leaf bases and fibrous tissue, topped by a crown of pinnate leaves, each leaf divided into many narrow leaflets along a central rib and armed at the base with sharp spines. The crown is the palm's factory: fronds capture sunlight, and new fronds emerge from the growing point at the top while old fronds are pruned away, leaving the characteristic patterned stem. Below ground, the palm grows a fibrous root system that spreads widely rather than driving one deep taproot down. That spread suits oasis and irrigated soils, where water arrives at the surface and in shallow channels, and it also helps the palm anchor itself against wind. Roots tolerate saline soils better than most fruit trees, a trait that matters in arid regions where irrigation water itself carries salts. Date palms are dioecious, meaning male and female flowers grow on separate plants. Flower clusters, called spathes, branch from the axils of leaves that emerged the previous year, and the female clusters, once pollinated, develop into the hanging bunches of dates. A single date is a drupe: a fleshy fruit around one seed, usually oblong and a few centimetres long, ripening from green through yellow or red to brown depending on variety.

title: Pollination of the Date Palm
description: Because male and female flowers grow on separate plants, a date grove needs both sexes, and under cultivation the female flowers are usually pollinated by hand. Growers keep far fewer male palms than female palms, commonly about one male to several dozen females, and they carry pollen from the male flower clusters to the female clusters during the short flowering window. Hand pollination gives growers control over which pollen fertilises which female, which keeps a named cultivar true to type, since seed-grown palms do not reliably repeat the parent's fruit. In the wild, wind also moves pollen, and traditional groves sometimes relied on wind and insects alone, but yields and fruit set are less predictable that way. Modern practice therefore treats pollination as a scheduled task: watch for the spathe to open, collect fresh male flowers, dust or insert pollen strands into the female cluster, and then thin the developing bunches so the remaining fruit grows large and unbruised. Bagging bunches early also protects them from birds and insects. Timing matters more than quantity. Pollen applied too early or too late sets fewer fruit, and a missed flowering season cannot be recovered until the next year. That is why the pollination record in a well-run grove reads like a calendar: variety, palm, date of flowering, pollen source, and result, all kept so the next season's plan improves on the last.

title: Major Date Cultivars: Ajwa, Medjool, Deglet Noor, Barhi, Khalas, and Sukkari
description: Ajwa is a soft, dark date associated with the Medina region, valued for a rich, caramel-like sweetness and a soft, almost melting texture when ripe. Medjool originated in Morocco and is now grown widely; it is large, very soft, and richly sweet, and a single pitted Medjool weighs about 24 grams, so four make roughly 100 grams. Deglet Noor, the golden semi-dry date of Tunisia and Algeria, is smaller and firmer, with a pitted date weighing about 7.1 grams, so about fourteen make 100 grams, and it holds its shape well in cooking and packing. Barhi is eaten at two stages: fresh and yellow, when it is crisp and mild, and fully ripe, when it turns brown and soft. Fresh Barhi carries far fewer calories per 100 grams than dried dates because of its higher water content, roughly 150 calories per 100 grams fresh against about 277 to 282 for dried Medjool and Deglet Noor. Khalas, widely grown in the Gulf, is a medium, reddish-brown date with a balanced sweetness and a firm-soft texture that keeps well. Sukkari, whose name recalls sweetness, is a soft, golden-brown Saudi date, often eaten fresh or semi-dried and prized for a honeyed flavour. Nutrition figures vary with moisture, so this record states the published USDA FoodData Central values as a range anchor: about 277 kilocalories per 100 grams for Medjool and about 282 for Deglet Noor, with roughly 75 grams of carbohydrate, 63 to 67 grams of sugars, 7 to 8 grams of fibre, and about 660 to 700 milligrams of potassium per 100 grams. No single figure covers every cultivar, every harvest, or every drying method, and fresh dates always sit lower in calories per gram than the same variety dried.

title: Cultivation of the Date Palm in Arabia
description: In Arabia the date palm is grown in oases, irrigated valleys, and planned groves, wherever groundwater or channel water can reach the roots through the long hot season. Growers plant offshoots, the suckers that arise near the base of a parent palm in its early years, rather than seeds, because an offshoot is already female, already the named cultivar, and already several years ahead of a seedling. Offshoots are removed when they are three to six years old and have formed roots of their own, then planted out and watered heavily until established. Spacing balances light, air, and water: palms planted too close shade each other and compete for water, while palms planted too far apart waste irrigated land. A common working spacing is around 8 to 10 metres between palms, giving roughly 100 to 150 palms per hectare, with the exact figure set by variety vigour, soil, and irrigation method. Between the palms, growers often plant lower crops that tolerate partial shade, so the grove works as a layered garden rather than a single-crop field. Arabian groves face heat, wind, and salt, and their management answers each in turn: mulch and basin irrigation hold moisture, windbreak plantings and the palms themselves break the wind, and drainage and leaching washes salts below the root zone. Harvest, pruning, and pollination are all climbing work on tall palms, so grove layout also has to leave room for ladders, lifting, and the safe lowering of heavy bunches.

title: Irrigation and Water Needs of the Date Palm
description: The date palm is drought-tolerant but not drought-loving: it survives dry conditions far better than most fruit trees, yet it only yields well when it receives steady water through fruit development. Published irrigation guidance therefore gives ranges, not a single number, because a young palm, a mature palm in full bearing, and a palm in a hot windy site drink very different amounts. A mature palm in a hot climate may use on the order of 150 to 300 litres per day in the peak season, with lower use in winter and higher use where soils are sandy and evaporation is high. Traditional irrigation floods basins around each palm or runs water through channels between rows, while modern groves increasingly use drip lines that place water directly at the root zone and cut evaporation losses. Drip systems also let growers feed water in small, frequent doses, which suits the palm's spreading fibrous roots and reduces the salt build-up that flood irrigation can leave behind when drainage is poor. Whichever method is used, drainage matters as much as supply: standing water rots roots, and salts must be washed below the root zone. Water planning for a grove is therefore arithmetic before it is plumbing: palms multiplied by litres per palm per day, multiplied by days, against the water the well or channel can actually deliver. A grove that cannot meet peak-season demand will still survive, but its bunches will be smaller, its fruit drier, and its yield far below the 40 to 80 kilograms per tree that well-watered palms reach. This record gives ranges and a calculator, not a prescription for any individual grove, because soil, climate, and variety change the true figure.

title: Harvest and Processing of Dates
description: Dates are harvested by hand, bunch by bunch, from ladders or lifting platforms, because a full bunch weighs 8 kilograms or more and the fruit bruises easily. Pickers judge ripeness by colour, softness, and taste, and a single bunch may be picked in several passes as individual dates ripen at different rates. Bunches are lowered carefully, not dropped, and damaged or insect-affected fruit is separated at the palm so it does not spoil the rest of the batch. After harvest, dates are sorted by size, colour, and moisture, then cleaned, graded, and packed. Some are sold fresh or semi-dried, some are dried further in sun or in controlled drying rooms until they reach a stable moisture level, and some are pitted and pressed into paste, blocks, or filled products. Drying concentrates the sugars, which is why dried dates are sweeter per gram and keep far longer than fresh dates, but over-drying hardens the flesh and dulls the flavour, so drying is stopped at a target moisture rather than run to completion. Storage is cool, dry, and pest-proof. Dates absorb odours and moisture from the air, so packed dates are kept sealed and away from strong smells, and commercial stores hold them at low temperature to slow sugar crystallisation and insect activity. The whole chain, from a bunch on a 20-metre palm to a sealed pack, is labour-intensive, which is part of why dates cost more than their weight in sugar alone would suggest.

title: Dates Nutrition: General Published Values
description: By published USDA FoodData Central values, 100 grams of dried dates carry about 277 kilocalories for Medjool and about 282 for Deglet Noor, with about 75 grams of carbohydrate, 63 to 67 grams of total sugars, 7 to 8 grams of dietary fibre, under half a gram of fat, and about 2 grams of protein. Potassium stands out among the minerals, at roughly 660 to 700 milligrams per 100 grams, with smaller amounts of magnesium, calcium, copper, and B vitamins, including niacin and pantothenic acid. Fresh dates carry fewer calories per gram because they hold more water, and values shift with variety, ripeness, and drying. Nutritionally, dates are best understood as concentrated fruit energy: mostly natural sugars with fibre, which slows eating and digestion compared with refined sugar alone, but they are still sugar-dense, so portions matter. A single Medjool at about 24 grams carries roughly 66 kilocalories, while a single Deglet Noor at about 7 grams carries roughly 20, which makes the per-piece difference between cultivars larger than the per-100-gram difference. Anyone using these figures for a personal diet should treat them as general published values, as of 2026-10-26, not as advice for an individual, and should check a current nutrition source for the exact product in hand. The glycemic picture is mixed and is stated here only in general terms: dates have a moderate glycemic index in published tables, but a single small serving raises blood sugar less than a large serving, and eating dates with fibre, protein, or fat alongside slows the rise. This record makes no health claim for any individual and no claim that dates treat any condition; it reports published composition values and leaves dietary decisions to the reader and their clinician.

title: Date Products: Syrup, Paste, Vinegar, and More
description: Beyond the whole fruit, dates become syrup, paste, vinegar, and alcohol-free fermented products, each using a different part of the fruit's character. Date syrup is made by simmering pitted dates in water, pressing, filtering, and thickening the liquid; it is used as a sweetener and spread, and its flavour is darker and more caramel-like than the fresh fruit. Date paste is pitted dates ground or pressed into a smooth block, used in baking and confectionery as a fruit-based sweetener and binder that holds moisture in cakes and bars. Date vinegar comes from fermenting date juice or syrup, first to an alcoholic stage and then to vinegar, and it is used in cooking and dressings in the same way as other fruit vinegars. Lower-grade fruit, trimmings, and pits feed other products: pits are ground for animal feed or roasted as a caffeine-free coffee substitute in some traditions, and the fibrous residue can be composted back into the grove. Nothing in a well-run date economy is thrown away quickly, because the fruit, the fibre, and the pit each have a use. Product quality follows fruit quality. Syrup from over-dried or damaged dates tastes harsh, paste from under-ripe dates lacks sweetness, and vinegar from contaminated juice spoils rather than ferments cleanly. That is why grading at harvest matters even for fruit destined for processing: the product cannot improve on the fruit it started from, and a processor's first job is sorting, not cooking.

title: Palm Pests and Diseases
description: The most destructive date palm pest worldwide is the red palm weevil, a beetle whose larvae tunnel inside the trunk, weakening the palm from within while the crown still looks healthy from outside. Early signs are subtle: oozing from the trunk, chewed fibres at the leaf bases, and a crown that wilts or collapses unevenly. Because the damage is internal, control depends on inspection, pheromone traps that catch adult weevils, and removal and destruction of heavily infested palms before the weevils spread to neighbours. Other pests include palm borers, scale insects, mites, and fruit moths, each attacking a different part of the palm or the bunch, and birds and rodents that damage ripening fruit. Diseases include bayoud, a fungal wilt that has devastated groves in North Africa, along with other fungal rots of the roots, trunk, and fruit, and a group of phytoplasma diseases that yellow and kill palms. No single spray answers all of these, and resistant varieties, clean planting material, quarantine on moved offshoots, and sanitation are the standing defences. The practical lesson is inspection before treatment. A grove walked regularly, with each palm looked at for frass, oozing, yellowing, and bunch damage, catches problems while they are still one palm's problem. A grove inspected only at harvest discovers problems when they are already a grove's problem, and the cost of that delay is measured in palms lost, not just in fruit lost.

title: Palm Crafts and Materials
description: Every part of the palm has a craft use. Fronds are split and woven into baskets, mats, trays, hats, and screens, and the midribs are bound into crates, fences, and light furniture. The fibrous sheath at the leaf bases is twisted into rope and cordage, the trunk is sawn into beams and planks for light construction, and the leaves, dried and bundled, thatch roofs and shade shelters. A palm grove is therefore also a materials store, and in many oasis communities the craft economy and the fruit economy grew up together. Craft quality follows material choice. Young green fronds bend without breaking and suit weaving, older dry fronds are stiffer and suit thatch and fencing, and trunk wood, being fibrous rather than true hardwood, suits light beams and boards but not heavy structural loads. Craftspeople sort material by age, dryness, and flexibility before they start, because a basket woven from the wrong fronds splits, and a roof thatched with green fronds shrinks and leaks as it dries. Modern craft keeps the same materials but adds new products: frond fibre pressed into boards, palm waste composted or burned as fuel, and decorative weaving sold beyond the oasis. The continuity is the point: the palm's craft uses are not a historical curiosity but a living materials system, and a grove managed for both fruit and fibre yields two incomes from the same trees.

title: Oases Ecology
description: An oasis is a fertile pocket in a desert where water reaches the surface, from a spring, a well, or a shallow water table, and the date palm is its keystone plant. The palm's crown shades the ground, cutting evaporation and cooling the air beneath it, and under that shade growers plant a second layer of fruit trees, then a third layer of vegetables and grains on the ground. That three-layer garden uses the same water three times over in effect, because shade from the top layer protects the layers below, and the whole system produces far more food per litre of water than a single exposed crop would. Oasis ecology is also a water story. Palms and their under-crops draw on groundwater that rain may take years or centuries to replace, so an oasis that pumps faster than its aquifer refills will shrink, and its palms will show the decline first as smaller bunches and then as dying crowns. Salts are the second slow threat: every litre of irrigation water leaves a little salt behind, and without drainage and periodic leaching, salts build up until the soil supports nothing. Sustainable oases therefore manage water and salt together, not water alone. Wildlife follows the water too. Oases shelter birds, insects, and small mammals that find food and shade nowhere else in the surrounding desert, and the palm groves act as stepping stones for migratory birds crossing arid regions. An oasis is not just a farm in a desert; it is an island ecosystem, and its health is read in its palms, its water table, its soil salts, and its birds together.

title: Palm Breeding and Research
description: Date palm breeding is slow because a palm takes 4 to 5 years to bear and 10 to 15 years to reach full bearing, so a breeder waits a decade to judge a single cross. Breeders therefore work with the tools that shorten the wait: selecting superior mother palms and their offshoots, crossing chosen males and females by hand pollination, and raising seedlings under observation for fruit quality, yield, disease resistance, and salt tolerance. Tissue culture now multiplies a chosen palm into many identical plantlets, which lets a good variety spread far faster than offshoots alone ever could, but it also demands laboratory care to keep the plantlets true to type. Research priorities follow the threats: resistance to bayoud wilt and to the red palm weevil, tolerance of salt and heat, and fruit that keeps well after harvest without losing flavour. Genomic studies map the palm's genes to traits like fruit colour, sugar composition, and ripening time, which helps breeders choose parents before the decade-long wait begins. None of this replaces the grove trial, because a palm that performs in a laboratory or a nursery must still prove itself in a real oasis, under real water limits and real pests. Gaps in the public record are stated plainly here: breeding results for many local cultivars are reported in regional journals and nursery catalogues rather than in one global register, so a complete worldwide list of bred varieties is not in the public record, and this record does not invent one. What is in the public record is the method, the timelines, and the named major cultivars, and those are what this record reports.

title: Palm Glossary
description: Bunch: the hanging cluster of dates that develops from one pollinated female flower cluster; a bunch may hold more than 1,000 dates and weigh 8 kilograms or more. Cultivar: a named, cultivated variety, kept true by vegetative propagation from offshoots or tissue culture, never reliably from seed. Dioecious: having male and female flowers on separate plants, so a grove needs both sexes. Drupe: a fleshy fruit with a single seed, the botanical description of a date. Frond: a large pinnate palm leaf, divided into leaflets along a central rib. Offshoot: a sucker arising near the base of a parent palm, removed at three to six years old with its own roots for planting. Pollination: the transfer of pollen from a male flower to a female flower, done by hand in most commercial groves. Spathe: the protective sheath around a flower cluster, which splits open at flowering. Tamar: the fully ripe, soft, dried stage of a date, as opposed to the earlier crisp and semi-ripe stages. Where a term also carries a traditional meaning, the tradition entry in this pair states that meaning separately and labels it tradition. This glossary is a finding aid, not a textbook: each entry gives the working meaning used in this pair, and the full treatment lives in the record named in the entry's subject. Terms not in the public record as defined here are not invented for this glossary.
